h121.content:
On April 24, 1646, sixty-three Orthodox priests of the Carpathian region gathered at the castle chapel of Uzhhorod and professed their faith in communion with the Pope of Rome, keeping their Byzantine rite and customs.

This union gave birth to the Ruthenian Greek Catholic Church, which today has eparchies in Ukraine, Slovakia, Hungary, and the United States, where it is known as the Byzantine Catholic Church.

h122.content:
Pope Julius II commissioned Michelangelo, who considered himself a sculptor, to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. Working on scaffolds for four years, he painted more than three hundred figures: the creation of the world, the fall, Noah, and the prophets and sibyls who foretold Christ.

Decades later, Michelangelo painted the Last Judgment on the altar wall. Popes are still elected beneath these frescoes in the conclave.

h123.content:
During the Reign of Terror of the French Revolution, the sixteen Discalced Carmelite nuns of Compiègne refused to abandon their religious life. They were condemned as "fanatics" and guillotined in Paris on July 17, 1794.

They went to the scaffold singing the Veni Creator, renewing their vows one by one. Ten days later the Terror ended with the fall of Robespierre. Beatified in 1906, they were declared saints by Pope Francis in 2024.

h124.content:
Pope Pius VII had made a concordat with Napoleon in 1801 and even attended his coronation in 1804. But when the pope refused to join Napoleon’s blockade against Britain, French troops occupied Rome, and in 1809 they arrested the pope and carried him off as a prisoner.

For nearly five years Pius VII was held at Savona and Fontainebleau, often isolated and pressured. He returned to Rome in triumph in 1814, after Napoleon’s fall, and later gave shelter to Napoleon’s family.

h125.content:
On September 20, 1870, Italian troops breached the walls of Rome at the Porta Pia, and the Papal States, which had existed for more than a thousand years, came to an end. Pope Bl. Pius IX refused to accept the loss and withdrew into the Vatican.

For almost sixty years the popes called themselves "prisoners in the Vatican," until the Lateran Treaty of 1929 created Vatican City as a small independent state, guaranteeing the pope’s freedom.

h126.content:
For centuries the laws of the Church were scattered across many collections. Pope St. Pius X began the work of gathering them into a single code, and Pope Benedict XV promulgated the first Code of Canon Law in 1917.

After the Second Vatican Council, Pope St. John Paul II promulgated a revised Code for the Latin Church in 1983, and in 1990 the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches, the first common law for all the Eastern Catholic Churches.
